response.query: Which preprocessing pipelines (specific atmospheric correction, cloud/shadow masking, radiometric normalization, SAR speckle filters, LiDAR DTM/CHM steps) yield reliable multi-sensor fusion?
response.answer: Reliable multi-sensor fusion uses atmospheric correction, radiometric normalization, and SAR speckle filtering. LiDAR DTM/CHM steps are also crucial for accurate terrain representation. These preprocessing steps ensure data comparability across different sensors and conditions.

results.title: [PDF] Chapter 4. Preprocessing in remote sensing
results.content: For example, early image analysis in remote sensing often directly employed the digital numbers (DNs) produced by the sensor to estimate land surface variables like Leaf Area Index (LAI). This means that when you would like to compare remote sensing images, taken at different observation dates and times (different atmospheric conditions) and at different altitudes with different sensor systems, then preprocessing must be performed. 4.3 Radiometric correction The radiance measured by a sensor (Figure 4.2) for a specific object on the earth is influenced by factors as changes in scene illumination, atmospheric conditions, viewing geometry, and instrument response characteristics. In this paragraph we will explain the different steps of the radiometric correction process which are dependent upon the characteristics of the sensor used to acquire the image data. Another radiometric data processing step required for quantitative applications is the process that converts recorded sensor digital numbers to an absolute scale of radiance (watts per steradian per square meter) which is independent of the image forming characteristics of the sensor (e.g., integration time, band centre, intensity of input signal). 4.5 Atmospheric correction As indicated in Figure 4.1, the composition of the atmosphere has an important effect on the measurement of radiance with remote sensing. The final result of an atmospheric correction procedure are surface reflectance values for all image pixels which can be used for further image processing, e.g., classification and variable estimation (LAI). 8 Figure 4.5: Example of Landsat TM image before (left) and after (right) atmospheric correction (from Liang et al., 2001) 4.6 Geometric correction The previous paragraphs have mainly focused on correction of remote sensing images in the spectral domain. 10 4.7 Recent developments in preprocessing With the increasing use of remote sensing for global monitoring of the earth (e.g., using the medium resolution MODIS and MERIS sensors), it becomes very important to know the quality of the images that are acquired and compared with each other. This means that for a specific remote sensing sensor automated processing chains are developed that process the acquired images from raw data to surface reflectance and finally to a set of higher order products (NDVI, LAI, albedo etc.).

results.title: [PDF] Radiometric Normalizationradiometric normalization Further Readings
results.content: Radiometric Normalizationradiometric normalization Remote sensing applications often use image time series or mosaics of various images or image parts. Radiometric normalization generally refers to empirically reducing the differences between images in time series or mosaics related to differences in the image acquisition time or date. Radiometric normalization is applied both to images that have undergone atmospheric correction and to those that have not. Radiometric normalization may also be unnecessary when using machine-learning models, to classify an image mosaic, if the reference data for the classification model represent all image dates. To radiometrically normalize images to a reference image or to each other, calibration models are estimated from pixels in the images and then applied to the imagery. results.title: Radiometric Correction: Significance and symbolism
results.content: # Significance of Radiometric Correction. Radiometric correction is a crucial preprocessing step for remotely sensed data like Sentinel-2 A imagery. It calibrates satellite images by converting digital numbers to top-of-atmosphere reflectance. This process adjusts for sensor and atmospheric effects to reduce radiometric errors and improve data quality. The goal is to ensure accurate reflectance values for subsequent classification and analysis, making it an essential step in remote sensing workflows. Synonyms: Calibration, Adjustment, Normalization, Rectification, Processing, Refinement, Atmospheric correction, Image calibration, Data normalization. The below excerpts are indicatory and do represent direct quotations or translations. It is your responsibility to fact check each reference. ## The concept of Radiometric Correction in scientific sources. Radiometric Correction is a crucial preprocessing step for satellite imagery, like Sentinel-2 A, that calibrates data by converting digital numbers to top-of-atmosphere reflectance, reducing errors and ensuring accurate reflectance values for analysis. (1) Radiometric correction is a pre-processing step that adjusts the pixel values in remote sensing data to correct for sensor errors and atmospheric effects. (2) Radiometric correction was initially preprocessed for, and atmospheric correction to correct Landsat data for all of the years. (3) It is quantitative monitoring of the coastal seabed where plants grow, taking into account noise contributions from water column and adjacency effects. (4) Radiometric correction is the process of correcting errors in the brightness values of remotely sensed data, establishing a direct link between data and biophysical processes. (5) This is a process applied to satellite images to correct for sensor and atmospheric effects, ensuring accurate reflectance values for land cover classification.

New Spectral Indices – expanded library for optical workflows. # Sentinel 1A preprocessing steps. since i am new to the processing of sar data, i got a few questions about this topic. I want to use Sentinel 1A GRD data as a byproduct for a land use/ land cover study along with the Sentinel 2A data. Until now I found out that I basically need the following steps:. 1: calibration of the DNs to Sigma0, which should deliver the appropriate backscatter values (?) (Radar > Radiometric > Calibrate). Do I need to check the “save as complex” and perform the conversion “Linear to dB”? 2: despeckle (Radar > Speckle Filtering > Single Product Speckle Filter). Is there any other step necessary to perform the preprocessing? GRD-products are not complex (like SLC-products) so no need to save as complex. Linear-to-dB should be performed after speckle-filtering, not before it. You might want to consider using a co-registered stack of GRD-images, in which case you can perform multi-temporal filtering for speckle reduction. So I guess that my backscatter values of Sigma0 derived from the “linear to dB” conversion would correspond to the reflectance values in optical remote sensing. I also read about the radiometric normalization that can be performed during the terrain correction. Is this a common preprocessing step? Radiometric normalization is common and helpful in hilly areas. Radiometric terrain flattening works even better for diminishing topographic effects on SAR imagery. I have some questions about SAR prepossessing steps; actually I do not know what processes should I apply on those products;. I have GRD product, I saw in below link that ‘radiometric correction’ and ‘multilooking’ have been applied before on SAR images, what is left? B. Terrain correction (Although we do not need this step, if we are doing processing on ice). Is there any extra steps that I have to apply and why? 4.
